heading: The Aim API
textContent: Welcome back, Protag ! The spell lets you point at a spot in the world with your cursor and turn that click into a position your spell can use. It's a perfect companion for targeting other spells like the Projectile or Fire APIs.

heading: The Air API
textContent: Welcome back, Protag ! The spell is wind magic — it lets you shove entities around with a sudden air burst . Launch yourself across a gap, knock an enemy off a ledge, or break a fall, all with a single gust.

heading: The Earth API

Hand it a polygon, a rectangle, a circle, or let the player draw the outline by hand — the block springs into the world, ready to support, block, or bury. heading: Breaking down what we just did.
headingPath: Breaking down what we just did.
textContent: When the computer encounters this line of JavaScript, it is evaluated progressively. First, the computer sees the symbol. The JavaScript inerpreter looks that up from a table of known symbols, called a "scope" (in this case, the "global scope" - more on that later), and identifies as an Object. As such, when it sees the next character, , the language's logic dictates that we are requesting access to a property of the Object . Objects are basically little tables key-value pairs . Each key-value pair combines a key, typically a word (which we refer to more formally as a "string"), and a value, which is any kind of data you wish to associate with it. As for our object, its property is what is called a . A Function is a reusable block of code that performs - you guessed it - a function. Functions can accept input, which we call "arguments", and produce results, which we call "returning" a value. The function is a special function that accepts data and copies it into the program's output. Now that the computer knows it is calling a function, it needs to know what data is being passed in. In this case, it's going to be a String with the data "hello world". We know it's a string because it is in quotes - if we left the quotes off, we'd be telling the computer to look up the "hello" symbol in the current scope and we'd get an error. More on that later. For now, we provide "hello world", an acceptable string, and can observe the function acting upon it. Finally, we include a semicolon at the end of the line to tell the language the line is a discrete statement.
